title: The call from Safa
hookLine: he climbs Safa and asks, would you believe me if I said an army was behind this hill

cards: Ya sabahah! The cry goes up from the little hill of Safa. It's the alarm call, the one people shout when raiders are coming at dawn.

Men drop what they're doing and come running; those who can't come send someone to find out. The clans of Quraysh gather at the foot of the hill and look up. Standing on top is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.
The quiet season is over. Today: nadhir.

teach.h: HE CALLS THE CLANS BY NAME.
teach.b: Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the scene from Ibn Abbas. When the verse came, warn thy nearest kin, he climbed Safa and called the clans by name. When they had gathered, he began not with a sermon but with a question.
If I told you that horsemen in the valley were about to attack you, would you believe me?

teach.h: YOU HAVE ONLY TOLD THE TRUTH.
teach.b: They answered: yes, we have only ever known you to tell the truth. Then he said: I am a warner to you, before a severe punishment. Look at how he builds it.
He lets the city testify to his honesty before he says a single new thing. Years of trust, from the market, from the black stone, from Khadijah's caravans, are called in with one question.
And the word he uses for himself is nadhir, a warner. Not a ruler, not a fortune-teller. Someone who has seen what's coming and shouts so others can get ready, the way the alarm call itself works.
It is a word the Qur'an also uses for him. The report also says that one voice in the crowd answered him with a curse. Who it was, and what came back, is tomorrow.
Today, hold the question: would you believe me? It asks what kind of life makes a person believable when it matters.

how: Muslims retell the call from Safa as the beginning of the public message in Mecca; pilgrims on Hajj and Umrah walk between Safa and Marwah, though that rite remembers Hajar, not this day.

o: a ruler who commands the clans of Mecca
a warner, who shouts so others can get ready
a fortune-teller who reads what's coming

games.q: the call from Safa — tap the pairs.

s: he began with a long sermon
he began with a question: would you believe me?
the clans answered that they had only known him to tell the truth
he let them say it before he said anything new.
he called himself a warner, nadhir.

games.q: you're on Safa with the clans below you. how do you begin?
o: with a list of their wrongs.
with a question about whether they trust you.
games.why: he asked: if I told you riders were coming, would you believe me? only after their yes did he call himself a warner.

practice: Think of one true thing you've been softening or wrapping in extra words, a no, an apology, a concern, a thank-you, and find the plainest way to say it: one sentence, no decorations, repeated silently until it sounds clean.
If you pray, ask for the courage to say it well, when it's safe and kind to say.

wordCard.voice: Nadhir, a warner. The Prophet climbs Safa, asks the clans if they'd believe him, and names himself one who warns of what's coming. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a warner, one who warns of danger ahead; the word he used for himself on Safa.

carryVoice: Your line: would you believe me? A plain word keeps a person believable. Day seven hundred thirty-two.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4770 (Ibn Abbas: Safa; 'would you believe me?'; 'I am a warner to you')
